name: Lookups in a turned ring buffer
brief:
A ring buffer holds distinct order ids that were stored in rising order, but the read pointer has moved, so `ring` is that sorted list turned round at some point (perhaps not at all). For each id in `targets`, find its position in `ring`, or `-1` if it is absent.

Write `find_in_ring(ring, targets)`, which returns the positions in the order of `targets`.

Example. For `ring = [40, 50, 10, 20, 30]` and `targets = [20, 45]` the id 20 sits at position 3 and 45 is absent. The answer is `[3, -1]`.
constraints: $0 \le n, q \le 100{,}000$; ids are distinct whole numbers between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(\log n)$ time per lookup is the target. Scanning the ring for each id is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: First find where the smallest id sits with one binary search against the last entry. Then search the sorted order as if it started there, taking positions modulo `n`.

examples.note: The sorted order starts at position 2; 20 is its second id.
A ring not turned at all is plain sorted; 0 is absent.

tests.call: (lambda r: (len(r), sum(r), r.count(-1)))(find_in_ring([2 * ((i + 61729) % 100000) for i in range(100000)], [(i * 7919) % 200000 for i in range(100000)]))

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Comparing with the last entry tells which side of the turn `mid` is on, even when there is no turn.
Comparing with the first entry fails on a ring that was never turned: every entry is at least the first.
One $O(\log n)$ search finds the turn and one more answers each lookup.

planted.slip: It scans the ring for every id, which is $O(nq)$.
It tests the left half with `<` where `<=` is needed, so when `lo` meets `mid` it searches the wrong half.
It finds the turn by comparing with the first entry, which puts the start at the end when the ring is not turned.
